fixes.answer: This is a difficult question with no perfect answer. I believe very young children should have extremely limited screen time, as their development depends on [[real-world play]] and interaction. As they grow, technology can be gradually introduced, ideally in an educational and supervised way. So rather than a strict age, I favour a [[gradual]], [[age-appropriate]] approach, always emphasising quality of content over quantity of time.

The potential effects are concerning. Excessive screen time seems to be linked to problems with sleep, attention and physical health due to [[inactivity]]. It may also [[hinder]] the development of social skills and language if it replaces real interaction. There are concerns about exposure to unsuitable content too. So while technology has benefits, an excess can genuinely [[impair]] a child's healthy development, both physically and socially.
fixes.why: 'excess' is plain; marked 'inactivity'; softened the health claim

fixes.answer: Almost certainly, yes. As technology becomes ever more woven into every aspect of life, future generations will grow up with it as an [[inseparable]] part of their existence. This dependence will likely deepen, which brings both opportunities and risks. My hope is that alongside this, we will develop a stronger culture of digital wellbeing, teaching children to use technology [[intentionally]] and to maintain a healthy balance rather than being [[consumed]] by it.

Parents can take several practical steps. Using [[parental controls]] and age-appropriate settings helps filter unsuitable content. Keeping devices in shared family spaces rather than bedrooms allows for supervision. Most importantly, maintaining open, honest communication so children feel able to report anything [[troubling]] is vital. Educating children about online risks, like strangers and scams, [[empowers]] them. Ultimately, a combination of supervision and education is the best protection.
fixes.why: 'supervision' and 'education' are plain; marked 'parental controls' and 'troubling'

fixes.answer: The advantages are significant. Coding teaches [[logical thinking]], problem-solving and creativity, and it [[equips]] children with a highly valuable skill for the future job market. It can also be genuinely fun and empowering. The potential disadvantages are that it adds to screen time and academic pressure, and it should not [[crowd out]] other essential activities like play and physical exercise. So it is a valuable skill, provided it is kept in balance and not forced.
fixes.why: 'balance' and 'forced' are plain; marked 'logical thinking' and 'equips'

fixes.answer: I partly agree, though I think it is a little [[overstated]]. There is a legitimate concern that excessive screen time is replacing the outdoor play, imagination and face-to-face friendships that define a healthy childhood. However, technology also offers genuine benefits and is simply the reality of the modern world. So rather than [[demonising]] it, I believe the answer lies in [[moderation]], ensuring children still enjoy a rich, balanced upbringing.
